title: The Moonstone
author: Wilkie Collins
setting: Seringapatam in 1799, then a house on the Yorkshire coast and London in 1848–49, and finally Kattiawar in 1850
lengthNote: Around 195,000 words, written for thirty-two weekly instalments and divided among eleven separate narrators
openingLine: I address these lines⁠—written in India⁠—to my relatives in England.
summary: A diamond taken during the storming of Seringapatam arrives in a Yorkshire drawing room as a birthday present and vanishes the same night. Collins gives the case to eleven witnesses in turn, each writing to order and each certain of a different thing, so the mystery is solved less by a detective than by comparing accounts that do not fit. The solution turns on a dose of laudanum given without the patient’s knowledge, and the stone goes back to India.
referenceStyle: period and narrative, with the chapter where a narrative is divided

sourceText.label: Standard Ebooks text of The Moonstone
sourceText.note: A proofed transcription of Collins’s text. References follow the book’s own divisions — Prologue, First Period, the numbered Narratives of the Second Period, and Epilogue — with no running chapter count.

atAGlance.label: Serialised
atAGlance.note: Thirty-two weekly instalments in Dickens’s All the Year Round, and simultaneously in Harper’s Weekly.

atAGlance.label: First edition
atAGlance.note: Tinsley Brothers, three volumes, published in London before the serial had finished running.

atAGlance.label: Narrators
atAGlance.note: All writing to Franklin Blake’s commission, each confined to what they personally saw.

atAGlance.label: Historical anchor
atAGlance.note: The prologue places the theft during a documented assault of the Fourth Anglo-Mysore War.

structure.label: Prologue
structure.title: The Storming of Seringapatam (1799)
structure.summary: An unnamed cousin writes to his family explaining why he will never speak to John Herncastle again. In the confusion of the sack he finds Herncastle with a torch and a bloody dagger and two dead Indians at his feet, and hears the third man curse the stone as he dies. Nothing is proved, and the letter is deliberately left as a private accusation.

scenes.title: A letter that accuses nobody in public
scenes.summary: The legend of the yellow diamond, its removal from Somnauth, and a death in a doorway that the writer will not report to his colonel.

structure.label: First Period
structure.title: The Loss of the Diamond (1848), told by Gabriel Betteredge
structure.summary: The house steward writes twenty-three chapters of the birthday, the theft and the investigation, in a voice built out of Robinson Crusoe, household hierarchy and an unshakeable belief that women are the cause of most trouble. Sergeant Cuff arrives, reads the smeared paint on a door correctly and the people entirely wrongly, Rosanna Spearman drowns herself in the quicksand, and Rachel leaves in a fury nobody can explain.

scenes.title: The steward sets the scene
scenes.summary: Betteredge is commissioned to write, opens Robinson Crusoe for guidance, and introduces the household, Lady Verinder and the Shivering Sand.

scenes.title: The diamond arrives
scenes.summary: Franklin Blake brings the legacy from the wicked Colonel; three Indian jugglers appear at the gate; Rachel is given the stone on her eighteenth birthday.

scenes.title: The night and the morning after
scenes.summary: The dinner party, Murthwaite’s warning, the missing diamond, the local superintendent’s failure, and the sending for Sergeant Cuff.

scenes.title: Cuff’s investigation
scenes.summary: The smeared door, the missing nightgown, Cuff’s theory of Rachel’s debts, and Rosanna’s journey to Frizinghall and to the sand.

scenes.title: The case abandoned
scenes.summary: Rosanna drowns, Rachel refuses to be questioned, Cuff is dismissed with three predictions, and Franklin Blake leaves England.

structure.label: Second Period, First Narrative
structure.title: Contributed by Miss Clack
structure.summary: A poor relation with a bag of religious tracts takes the story to London, and reveals far more than she intends. Miss Clack is present at Godfrey Ablewhite’s proposal, at Rachel’s refusal and at Lady Verinder’s death, and reports all three through a haze of self-congratulation. Collins prints Franklin Blake’s letters declining her extracts inside her own narrative, so the reader watches her being edited.

scenes.ref: Second Period, First Narrative, Chapters I–III
scenes.title: Tracts and a proposal
scenes.summary: Clack distributes improving literature, hides behind a curtain, and hears Godfrey Ablewhite propose to Rachel.

scenes.ref: Second Period, First Narrative, Chapters IV–VI
scenes.title: A will and a death
scenes.summary: Lady Verinder’s illness and will; Clack’s campaign of anonymous extracts; the correspondence in which Blake refuses to print them.

scenes.ref: Second Period, First Narrative, Chapters VII–VIII
scenes.title: The engagement broken
scenes.summary: Rachel breaks with Godfrey once his father’s inquiries are made, and Clack records his composure as saintliness.

structure.label: Second Period, Second Narrative
structure.title: Contributed by Mathew Bruff, Solicitor
structure.summary: The family lawyer supplies what only a lawyer would have: the terms of Lady Verinder’s will, the reason Godfrey’s interest in Rachel cooled, and an interview with an Indian client who wanted to know the law on pledged property. Bruff is shrewd, useful and quite sure that women cannot administer a trust, which is the kind of blind spot Collins gives to every witness.

scenes.ref: Second Period, Second Narrative, Chapter I
scenes.title: The will
scenes.summary: Rachel has only a life interest, which removes Godfrey’s motive for marrying her and supplies Bruff’s explanation of his conduct.

scenes.ref: Second Period, Second Narrative, Chapters II–III
scenes.title: The diamond in the bank
scenes.summary: A question about the Indian law of pledges, and Murthwaite’s reading of the conspiracy at a London dinner table.

structure.label: Second Period, Third Narrative
structure.title: Contributed by Franklin Blake
structure.summary: Blake returns, commissions the whole record, and follows Rosanna’s posthumous letter to a tin box buried under the Shivering Sand. In it is a paint-stained nightgown marked with his own name. He then hears from Rachel that she watched him take the diamond with her own eyes, and from then on the novel’s central problem is a contradiction, not a mystery.

scenes.ref: Second Period, Third Narrative, Chapters I–III
scenes.title: The buried box
scenes.summary: Betteredge, the quicksand, the chain, and a nightgown that carries the wrong name — his own.

scenes.ref: Second Period, Third Narrative, Chapters IV–VII
scenes.title: Rosanna’s letter and Rachel’s evidence
scenes.summary: Rosanna’s account of her silence and her love; Rachel, confronted at last, says she saw him do it.

scenes.ref: Second Period, Third Narrative, Chapters VIII–X
scenes.title: Ezra Jennings
scenes.summary: Mr. Candy’s wandering memory, and an assistant nobody in the town will speak to, who has the means of reconstructing what was said at the birthday dinner.

structure.label: Second Period, Fourth Narrative
structure.title: Extracted from the Journal of Ezra Jennings
structure.summary: A dying man with a disgraced past and an opium habit designs the experiment that solves the case: reproduce the conditions of the birthday night, give the same dose, and see what Blake does. The journal is the most intimate document in the book, and it is kept by the only narrator who has nothing to gain and no reputation to protect.

scenes.title: The reconstruction
scenes.summary: Consent obtained from Rachel and Mr. Bruff, the house restored to its 1848 state, the laudanum given, and Blake watched through the night.

structure.label: Second Period, Fifth to Eighth Narratives
structure.title: Blake resumed, Cuff, Mr. Candy and Betteredge
structure.summary: The experiment proves what Blake did and not where the diamond went, so the last movement follows the stone to a London bank, a disguise and a murder in a cheap tavern. Sergeant Cuff returns to write out the case he got wrong, naming a man whose reputation for charity had been paid for out of a trust he had robbed. Betteredge closes the book with Robinson Crusoe, as he opened it.

scenes.title: The pursuit to London
scenes.summary: The pledged diamond, the watch on the bank, and a bearded man followed to a tavern in Shore Lane.

scenes.title: Contributed by Sergeant Cuff
scenes.summary: Cuff’s written account of Godfrey Ablewhite’s two lives, the trust he had emptied, and the debt the diamond was raised to pay.

scenes.title: In a Letter from Mr. Candy
scenes.summary: The doctor supplies the last medical detail and the news of Ezra Jennings’s death.

scenes.title: Contributed by Gabriel Betteredge
scenes.summary: The steward is given the last word, and uses it on a marriage, a baby and his own favourite book.

structure.label: Epilogue
structure.title: The Finding of the Diamond
structure.summary: Three short statements move the story out of English hands. Cuff’s man and a ship’s captain trace the three Indians as far as Bombay, and then Murthwaite, travelling in Kattiawar, watches a night ceremony at Somnauth and sees the yellow diamond back in the forehead of the god. The English narrators complete their record and lose the object it was about.

scenes.title: The Statement of Sergeant Cuff’s Man (1849)
scenes.summary: Three Hindus board a steamer bound for Rotterdam and are followed no further.

scenes.title: The Statement of the Captain (1849)
scenes.summary: Three passengers go overboard off the Indian coast and swim for the shore.

scenes.title: The Statement of Mr. Murthwaite (1850)
scenes.summary: A pilgrimage at Somnauth, three penitents parting for ever, and the Moonstone restored to the god of the Moon.

characters.name: Gabriel Betteredge
characters.role: House steward at Lady Verinder’s, and first narrator
characters.summary: Seventy years old, in service since he was a footman, and entirely convinced that a household runs on precedence and that Robinson Crusoe will answer any question put to it. His prejudices are visible on every page, which is precisely what makes his evidence usable: the reader can see the shape of what he is leaving out.
characters.clue: He has worn out six copies of one book, opens it at random whenever he needs advice, and calls his sudden interest in the investigation a disease.

characters.name: Rachel Verinder
characters.role: The owner of the diamond, on her eighteenth birthday
characters.summary: She is the only person in the book who knows a central fact from the first morning and refuses to give it up, and her silence is read by everyone as guilt, temper or debt. Collins gives her no narrative of her own, so she is constructed entirely out of other people’s accounts of a woman they have decided is behaving badly.
characters.clue: She saw the theft with her own eyes and will not say what she saw, because saying it would ruin the man she loves.

relationships.label: loves, and believes she saw steal the diamond

characters.name: Franklin Blake
characters.role: Lady Verinder’s nephew, and the compiler of the record
characters.summary: He brings the diamond from London, commissions every narrative in the book, and turns out to be the man who took it. Educated in Germany, France and Italy, he argues with himself in three national manners, and his greatest discovery is that his own memory holds nothing at all of the most important night of his life.
characters.clue: He collects everybody else’s testimony in order to find a thief, and finds his own name on the evidence.

characters.name: Rosanna Spearman
characters.summary: Taken from a reformatory, deformed in one shoulder, and in love with a gentleman who does not notice she exists. She hides the paint-stained nightgown to protect him, is suspected because of her record, and walks into the Shivering Sand. Her letter, read fifty chapters later, is the most painful document in the book.
characters.clue: A housemaid with a prison record and a crooked shoulder, who buries the evidence that would convict a man who has never once looked at her.

characters.name: Sergeant Cuff
characters.role: A detective officer from Scotland Yard
characters.summary: Grizzled, softly spoken and interested chiefly in roses, he reads a smear of paint faster than anybody and misreads a young woman completely. Collins makes him formidable and also wrong, which is unusual in the genre he helped invent: the great detective leaves the case with three predictions, two of which come true for reasons he never understood.
characters.clue: He whistles ‘The Last Rose of Summer’ when he is thinking, and means to give up catching thieves for a nursery garden.

characters.name: Drusilla Clack
characters.role: A poor cousin, and the second period’s first narrator
characters.summary: She lives on a small income in Brittany, distributes tracts with titles like ‘Satan in the Hair Brush’, and writes her narrative for the fee. Everything she reports is accurate and every judgement she attaches to it is wrong, which makes her the clearest demonstration of Collins’s method: evidence and interpretation arriving in the same sentence and needing to be separated by the reader.
characters.clue: She leaves improving pamphlets in hat-boxes and under sofa cushions, and hides behind a curtain to witness a proposal of marriage.
characters.firstAppearance: Second Period, First Narrative, Chapter I

characters.name: Godfrey Ablewhite
characters.role: A barrister and celebrated charitable speaker
characters.summary: The favourite of the Ladies’ committees, a large fair man who is kind to everybody and is living two lives at the expense of a trust he was supposed to hold. Collins makes him the one figure in the book whose public character is entirely manufactured, and the novel’s method — many witnesses, each partial — is exactly what is needed to catch him.
characters.clue: The ladies’ favourite platform speaker, whose charity is funded by a minor’s money he has already spent.

characters.name: Ezra Jennings
characters.role: Mr. Candy’s assistant, and the designer of the experiment
characters.summary: Of mixed birth, piebald hair, dying of an incurable disease and ruined years ago by an accusation he will not describe, he is the only person who will try an idea out before asserting it. He reconstructs the birthday night as a controlled trial and insists that Rachel’s consent be freely given, and he asks for nothing except to be remembered.
characters.clue: His hair is black on one side and white on the other, the town will not speak to him, and he keeps himself alive on the drug that solves the case.
characters.firstAppearance: Second Period, Third Narrative, Chapter IX

characters.name: Mathew Bruff
characters.summary: He drew Sir John’s will in ten minutes and has kept the family’s secrets ever since, and his narrative supplies the legal machinery the plot turns on. He is also the proof that competence is no protection against prejudice: he explains Rachel’s troubles shrewdly and states in the same breath that hardly one woman in a thousand could manage a trust.
characters.firstAppearance: Second Period, Second Narrative, Chapter I

characters.name: The three Indians
characters.role: Brahmin guardians of the Moonstone, travelling as jugglers
characters.summary: They appear at the gate, at a London bank and finally at Somnauth, and they are the only characters with a claim to the diamond that predates every English one. Collins filters them through Victorian conventions of mystery and disguise, and still gives them the last word: the stone goes home and the English lose sight of it for ever.

characters.name: Mr. Murthwaite
characters.role: A traveller in India, and the last witness
characters.summary: He is the only Englishman in the book who can speak to the three Indians in their own language and the only one who states plainly what they will do to recover the stone. His statement closes the novel from Kattiawar, which puts the final act of interpretation outside the English record entirely.

characters.name: Lady Julia Verinder
characters.role: Rachel’s mother, mistress of the house
characters.summary: She will not have her daughter questioned, sends Cuff away before he can go further, and dies before the case is reopened. Her judgement is the one the household runs on, and it is exercised in the teeth of the professional advice she is paying for.

themes.name: Testimony and its limits
themes.summary: Every narrator is instructed to write only what they saw, and every one of them breaks the rule by supplying motive. The novel is built so that the truth exists nowhere in a single document: it has to be assembled by a reader setting Betteredge’s prejudice against Clack’s piety against Bruff’s professional certainty.
themes.development: Betteredge establishes the method and its weakness; Clack pushes unreliability to comedy; Jennings’s journal is the one narrative with nothing to defend, which is why it can solve the case.

themes.name: Empire and possession
themes.summary: The stone is stolen twice — from Somnauth in the eleventh century and from Seringapatam in 1799 — before it becomes an English birthday present. Collins attaches the adjective ‘Indian’ to it in every drawing room and bank vault, so English law can hold the diamond but cannot naturalise it.
themes.development: A private letter of accusation in the Prologue, a legacy designed as a weapon in the First Period, and a restitution in the Epilogue that the English narrators can record but not control.

themes.name: Detection and its blind spots
themes.summary: Cuff reads objects brilliantly and people badly, and in the end the case is opened by an experiment, not by inference. The novel insists that clues belong to several disciplines — policing, medicine, law, household routine — and that a detective who owns only one of them will get it wrong.
themes.development: Local incompetence, then professional inference, then a collapse of the professional theory, and finally a reconstruction under laboratory conditions.

themes.name: Class, service and suspicion
themes.summary: Rosanna is suspected because she was a thief; the servants are examined first; Betteredge measures every visitor by the manner in which the household should receive them. The book is unusually clear that a criminal record and a crooked shoulder are treated as evidence, while a reputation for charity is treated as an alibi.
themes.development: The servants’ rooms are searched in the First Period; the man nobody suspects is exposed in the Sixth Narrative, by which time he has been dead for chapters.

themes.name: Memory, medicine and the unwitnessed act
themes.summary: The solution requires a state in which a man acts with purpose and retains nothing. Collins builds it out of contemporary argument about opium, nervous disease and the conditions under which an experiment can be repeated, and he is careful that the drug proves nothing on its own — Jennings has to design, observe and interpret.
themes.development: A dose given as a joke at the birthday dinner, a year of contradiction, and a second dose given deliberately with witnesses, consent and a written protocol.

themes.name: Respectability as a disguise
themes.summary: The novel’s two most public characters — a platform philanthropist and a tract-distributing spinster — are the ones least able to see themselves. Collins sets professed virtue against conduct repeatedly, and reserves his admiration for a reformed thief, a dying outcast and an old servant who admits he reads one book for comfort.
themes.development: Godfrey’s charity funds itself from a trust; Clack’s piety is paid for by the page; Jennings, whom nobody will speak to, is the only person who asks for consent before he acts.

techniques.name: Multiple narration
techniques.definition: A story assembled from separate first-person accounts, each limited to what the writer witnessed.
techniques.inThisBook: Eleven narrators write in turn to Franklin Blake’s commission, and none of them can revise another’s pages, so the contradictions stay on the record.

techniques.name: The documentary frame
techniques.definition: A novel presented as a dossier of letters, journals, statements and reports.
techniques.inThisBook: Blake’s commission is explained in Chapter I and the correspondence about what may be included is printed inside the narrative it belongs to.

techniques.name: The unreliable narrator
techniques.definition: A witness whose facts can be trusted and whose judgements cannot.
techniques.inThisBook: Miss Clack reports a proposal, a will and a death accurately while describing all three as tributes to her own Christian usefulness.

techniques.name: The material clue
techniques.definition: A physical trace that carries the solution before anybody can read it.
techniques.inThisBook: A smear in wet paint fixes the time, a buried nightgown fixes the name, and both are in the reader’s hands long before they are understood.

techniques.name: Serial suspense
techniques.definition: Structure shaped by weekly publication — withheld information, instalment endings, deliberate recurrence.
techniques.inThisBook: Thirty-two weeks meant readers had to carry a detail for months, so Collins brings back the quicksand, the paint and the Indians at intervals, since readers could not be relied on to remember.

techniques.name: Written voice
techniques.definition: Characterisation carried by the habits of a narrator’s prose, not by description.
techniques.inThisBook: Betteredge digresses and quotes Defoe, Clack italicises her own virtues, Bruff numbers his points, and Jennings writes in dated fragments between doses.

quotations.text: the Mohammedan conqueror, Mahmoud of Ghizni, crossed India; seized on the holy city of Somnauth; and stripped of its treasures the famous temple, which had stood for centuries⁠—the shrine of Hindu pilgrimage, and the wonder of the Eastern world.
quotations.context: The family legend of the diamond, as the letter-writer has heard it in camp.
quotations.analysis: The theft the English commit in 1799 is not the first: Collins puts an eleventh-century sack at the head of the book so that the stone arrives with a history of plunder already attached. The Epilogue returns to exactly this city, so the novel’s shape is a circle, not a chase.
quotations.source: Standard Ebooks text, Prologue

quotations.text: “The Moonstone will have its vengeance yet on you and yours!” He spoke those words, and fell dead on the floor.
quotations.context: The last of the three guardians, dying in the armoury doorway at Seringapatam.
quotations.analysis: The curse is the one supernatural claim in a novel that otherwise explains everything by paint, law and medicine, and Collins puts it in a language the narrator has to have translated for him. Every subsequent misfortune can be read as fulfilment or coincidence, and the book never adjudicates.
quotations.source: Standard Ebooks text, Prologue

quotations.text: In the first part of Robinson Crusoe, at page one hundred and twenty-nine, you will find it thus written:
quotations.context: The opening sentence of Betteredge’s narrative.
quotations.analysis: A detective novel begins by citing another book by page number, and the citation is exact where everything else in Betteredge’s testimony will be approximate. Collins is announcing his method in the first line: this story will arrive as a document that quotes its sources.
quotations.source: Standard Ebooks text, First Period, Chapter I

quotations.text: When my spirits are bad⁠—Robinson Crusoe. When I want advice⁠—Robinson Crusoe. In past times when my wife plagued me; in present times when I have had a drop too much⁠—Robinson Crusoe. I have worn out six stout Robinson Crusoes
quotations.context: Betteredge explaining what the book is for.
quotations.analysis: The list runs from low spirits to marital trouble to drink, and the remedy never changes; with six worn-out copies the joke becomes a portrait of a life. It also plants a foundational story of English trade and mastery inside a novel about stolen colonial property, and Collins leaves the reader to notice.
quotations.source: Standard Ebooks text, First Period, Chapter I

quotations.text: trembling in a manner most remarkable to see, and which has given to it, among the people in our parts, the name of the Shivering Sand.
quotations.context: Betteredge describing the quicksand in the little bay below the house.
quotations.analysis: The name comes from the local people, not from a map, so the place is real but slightly outside ordinary jurisdiction. The sand does the work a Gothic castle would once have done: it swallows a woman, hides the only physical evidence, and gives it back a year later intact.
quotations.source: Standard Ebooks text, First Period, Chapter IV

quotations.text: here was our quiet English house suddenly invaded by a devilish Indian Diamond⁠—bringing after it a conspiracy of living rogues, set loose on us by the vengeance of a dead man.
quotations.context: Betteredge taking in what Franklin Blake has just told him about the legacy.
quotations.analysis: The sentence sets ‘quiet English house’ against ‘devilish Indian Diamond’ as though the two belonged to different worlds, which is the assumption the whole novel dismantles. The conspiracy of living rogues turns out to include an English barrister, and the vengeance of a dead man to be an English colonel’s.
quotations.source: Standard Ebooks text, First Period, Chapter V

quotations.text: Send the Diamond tomorrow (under guard of more than one man) to be cut up at Amsterdam. Make half a dozen diamonds of it, instead of one. There is an end of its sacred identity as The Moonstone
quotations.context: Murthwaite’s advice at the birthday dinner on how to end the danger.
quotations.analysis: The one solution offered that would actually work is refused because it would destroy the value of the stone as a stone. Murthwaite has identified precisely what makes the object dangerous — its sacred identity — and the English response is to bank it instead, which guarantees the rest of the plot.
quotations.source: Standard Ebooks text, First Period, Chapter X

quotations.text: One of these days (please God) I shall retire from catching thieves, and try my hand at growing roses.
quotations.context: The Sergeant’s first conversation on arriving, conducted with the gardener about grass walks.
quotations.analysis: Collins gives his detective a private life before he gives him a theory, and the roses measure something: Cuff is at his most attentive and most accurate when the subject is not human. The same man will shortly read Rachel Verinder as a young woman in debt.
quotations.source: Standard Ebooks text, First Period, Chapter XII

quotations.text: “Nobody has stolen the Diamond,” answered Sergeant Cuff.
quotations.context: Overheard by Betteredge at the threshold, in reply to Franklin Blake’s question.
quotations.analysis: The line is the first statement of the book’s real problem, which is less who took it than whether taking it was a theft at all. Cuff means that Rachel has removed her own property to raise money; he is wrong about the person and right about the grammar, since the man who carried the diamond out of the room had no criminal intention either.
quotations.source: Standard Ebooks text, First Period, Chapter XII

quotations.text: If there is such a thing known at the doctor’s shop as a detective-fever, that disease had now got fast hold of your humble servant.
quotations.context: Following Cuff down to the beach on the track of Rosanna Spearman.
quotations.analysis: Betteredge coins the phrase to excuse himself, and it names something the novel makes formally true: once Cuff begins asking questions, every detail in the house looks like a clue and every servant like a suspect. The word ‘fever’ also carries the warning — the appetite for a solution is what produces the wrong one.
quotations.source: Standard Ebooks text, First Period, Chapter XV

quotations.text: having always a few tracts in my bag, I selected one which proved to be quite providentially applicable to the person who answered the door.
quotations.reference: Second Period, First Narrative, Chapter I
quotations.context: Waiting in the hall of her aunt’s London house.
quotations.analysis: The pamphlet is chosen for the servant who opened the door, which means a stranger has been diagnosed in the time it takes to cross a hall. Clack’s own word — providentially — does the work of concealing a judgement as a piece of divine good fortune, and she uses the same manoeuvre on every person in her narrative.
quotations.source: Standard Ebooks text, Second Period, First Narrative, Chapter I

quotations.text: The chapters best adapted to female perusal are “Satan in the Hair Brush;” “Satan behind the Looking Glass;” “Satan under the Tea Table;” “Satan out of the Window”
quotations.reference: Second Period, First Narrative, Chapter IV
quotations.context: Describing the book she leaves for Lady Verinder to find.
quotations.analysis: The comedy is in the domestic inventory — brush, looking glass, tea table, window — where the devil becomes one more piece of furniture. Collins is also making a point about method: Clack finds significance in ordinary household objects with exactly the confidence Sergeant Cuff brings to a smear of paint.
quotations.source: Standard Ebooks text, Second Period, First Narrative, Chapter IV

quotations.text: he will refrain from mentioning any personal objection which he may entertain to this species of literature
quotations.reference: Second Period, First Narrative, Chapter VI
quotations.context: One of the letters Collins prints inside Clack’s own narrative, refusing her extracts.
quotations.analysis: The editor of the record appears inside the record, and the reader watches the dossier being assembled and trimmed. Blake’s courtesy is lethal — he declines to mention his personal objection while mentioning it — and the exchange tells us, in passing, that every narrative in the book has passed through one man’s hands.
quotations.source: Standard Ebooks text, Second Period, First Narrative, Chapter VI

quotations.text: to be also capable of properly administering a trust (which, in my experience of the fair sex, not one in a thousand of them is competent to do)
quotations.reference: Second Period, Second Narrative, Chapter I
quotations.context: Explaining why Sir John’s will left everything to his wife.
quotations.analysis: The parenthesis is the whole point: Bruff praises Lady Verinder’s competence and generalises about her sex in the same sentence, without noticing the contradiction. Collins gives his most reliable witness a prejudice he cannot see, which is the exact defect the novel’s many-narrator structure exists to expose.
quotations.source: Standard Ebooks text, Second Period, Second Narrative, Chapter I

quotations.text: I looked back again at the letters. My own name. Plainly confronting me
quotations.reference: Second Period, Third Narrative, Chapter III
quotations.context: Opening the tin case recovered from under the Shivering Sand and reading the mark on the nightgown.
quotations.analysis: Collins breaks the paragraph into fragments so that the sentence has to be read twice, which is what Blake is doing on the page. The buried evidence solves the mystery and destroys the investigator in the same instant, and the novel still has three hundred pages to run.
quotations.source: Standard Ebooks text, Second Period, Third Narrative, Chapter III

quotations.text: And, on the unanswerable evidence of the paint-stain, I had discovered myself as the thief.
quotations.reference: Second Period, Third Narrative, Chapter III
quotations.context: The end of the same scene, with Betteredge walking towards him along the sand.
quotations.analysis: ‘Unanswerable’ is the word a lawyer would use, and Blake is applying the standard of proof he has been gathering testimony under. The sentence also fuses detective and criminal into one grammatical subject, which is the structural joke the entire second half depends on.
quotations.source: Standard Ebooks text, Second Period, Third Narrative, Chapter III

quotations.text: His gipsy-complexion, his fleshless cheeks, his gaunt facial bones, his dreamy eyes, his extraordinary parti-coloured hair, the puzzling contradiction between his face and figure which made him look old and young both together
quotations.reference: Second Period, Third Narrative, Chapter IX
quotations.context: Franklin Blake’s first close look at Mr. Candy’s assistant.
quotations.analysis: Blake catalogues the features that have made a whole town refuse to employ Jennings and admits that his own first impression is unfavourable. The doubleness — old and young, black hair and white — is the book’s picture of a man read wrongly by everybody, which is precisely the condition Rachel and Rosanna are also in.
quotations.source: Standard Ebooks text, Second Period, Third Narrative, Chapter IX

quotations.text: The one effectual palliative in my case, is⁠—opium. To that all-potent and all-merciful drug I am indebted for a respite of many years from my sentence of death.
quotations.reference: Second Period, Third Narrative, Chapter IX
quotations.context: Jennings explaining his own illness to Franklin Blake.
quotations.analysis: The drug that lost Blake a night of his life is the same drug keeping Jennings alive, and the man who explains it is speaking from inside the experiment he is about to run. Collins, who took laudanum himself for years, presents opium as neither a poison nor a miracle: it is a treatment with a stated limit.
quotations.source: Standard Ebooks text, Second Period, Third Narrative, Chapter IX

quotations.text: It leaves her entirely mistress of her own decision. If she consents to assist the experiment, she consents of her own free will
quotations.context: From Jennings’s journal, on the letter he has drafted asking Rachel to permit the experiment.
quotations.analysis: Consent is written into the protocol before the laudanum is measured, by the one character the town has decided is disreputable. Set it beside the birthday dinner, where the first dose was administered to Blake as a practical joke without his knowledge, and the novel’s moral arrangement is complete.
quotations.source: Standard Ebooks text, Second Period, Fourth Narrative

quotations.text: And there, in the forehead of the deity, gleamed the yellow Diamond, whose splendour had last shone on me in England, from the bosom of a woman’s dress!
quotations.context: Murthwaite at the shrine in Kattiawar, watching the curtain drawn aside.
quotations.analysis: The last time the diamond was described it was on a woman’s dress at a birthday party, and Collins puts both settings into one sentence so the reader makes the comparison. The stone has not been recovered by anybody in the English narrative; it has simply gone back to where the Prologue took it from.
quotations.source: Standard Ebooks text, Epilogue, III

quotations.text: So the years pass, and repeat each other; so the same events revolve in the cycles of time. What will be the next adventures of the Moonstone? Who can tell?
quotations.context: The last sentences of the book.
quotations.analysis: A detective novel ends on an open question, and the question is what happens next; who did it is settled. The cycle Collins describes is the one the Prologue began — conquest, theft, restitution, conquest — and because he leaves it open, the English part of the story is one episode, not the whole account.
quotations.source: Standard Ebooks text, Epilogue, III

timeline.label: The storming of Seringapatam
timeline.detail: British forces take the city in the Fourth Anglo-Mysore War; Collins places the theft of the diamond in the confusion of the assault.

timeline.label: Wilkie Collins born in London
timeline.detail: The son of the landscape painter William Collins, and later trained for the law at Lincoln’s Inn.

timeline.label: Collins meets Charles Dickens
timeline.detail: The beginning of a collaboration and a friendship that gave Collins his serial platforms.

timeline.label: The Woman in White begins in All the Year Round
timeline.detail: Collins’s first great multiple-narrator novel, and the commercial proof of the method used again here.

timeline.label: The Moonstone serialised
timeline.detail: Thirty-two weekly instalments from 4 January to 8 August, in All the Year Round and in Harper’s Weekly.

timeline.label: Three-volume edition published
timeline.detail: Tinsley Brothers issue the London book in July, before the weekly serial has finished.

timeline.label: Revised one-volume text
timeline.detail: Smith, Elder issue a revised text with a new preface for a different market and format.

timeline.label: Collins’s own dramatisation staged
timeline.detail: He adapted the novel for the theatre himself, cutting the many narrators that give the book its structure.

timeline.label: Collins dies in London
timeline.detail: He had used laudanum for years against the pain of rheumatic illness, as Ezra Jennings does in the novel.

timeline.label: First sound film version
timeline.detail: One of a long line of adaptations that keep the theft and drop most of the narrators.

timeline.label: BBC television serial
timeline.detail: The first of several British television versions to attempt the novel’s sequence of witnesses.

criticalViews.position: A founding text of the detective novel
criticalViews.summary: The country-house theft, the professional detective, the false suspect, the material clue and the final reconstruction are all here in one book, and much later crime fiction can be described in its terms.
criticalViews.counter: Prose mysteries and investigating figures existed before 1868, and the claim can flatten what is unusual here — a detective who is wrong, and a solution nobody deduces.

criticalViews.position: A novel about testimony, more than crime
criticalViews.summary: On this reading the subject is how evidence is produced: who is asked, what they are allowed to say, and how religion, class and vanity shape what a witness notices. The structure does the arguing, since no single document is sufficient.
criticalViews.counter: It risks treating the plot as a pretext, when Collins plainly took great care to make the mechanism of the theft work in medical and legal detail.

criticalViews.summary: The stone is taken by force, held under English law, and returned outside it, and the Prologue and Epilogue frame the domestic mystery with acts of conquest and restitution the English narrators cannot control.
criticalViews.counter: The Indian characters are still filtered through Victorian conventions of disguise and inscrutability, and they are given no narrative of their own in a novel made entirely of narratives.

essayQuestions.question: What does Collins gain, and what does he give up, by telling the story through many narrators?
essayQuestions.focus: Structure, testimony and the reader’s work
plan: Set out the commission in the First Period: each witness confined to what they personally saw.
Use Betteredge to show the method’s strength — visible prejudice makes the omissions legible.
Read Miss Clack as the limiting case, where accurate facts arrive wrapped in judgements nobody can accept.
Weigh the cost: Rachel, the person who knows most, is never given a narrative, and the Indians none at all.
Conclude on the work the form gives a reader that a single detective’s account would not.

essayQuestions.question: ‘Sergeant Cuff is the most impressive person in the book and he gets it wrong.’ Discuss.
plan: Establish his real competence: the paint, the timing, the missing garment, the deduction about the town.
Show where the inference fails and why — a theory of Rachel’s debts that fits everything except Rachel.
Examine the part played by Rosanna’s record and appearance in making the wrong suspect plausible.
Set his method against Ezra Jennings’s: inference from traces, versus an experiment designed to produce new evidence.
Assess the Sixth Narrative, where Cuff writes up the truth and thereby admits what his first theory cost.

essayQuestions.question: How far is the Prologue necessary to The Moonstone?
plan: Describe what the Prologue establishes: an eleventh-century sack, a documented 1799 assault, a private accusation, a curse.
Trace how Herncastle’s legacy works as a weapon, not a gift, and what that does to the birthday.
Follow the adjective ‘Indian’ through the English chapters, where the stone is repeatedly given a geography.
Read the Epilogue as the Prologue completed, and note that no English narrator is present for the restitution.
Decide whether the frame is a moral argument, an exotic device, or both.

essayQuestions.question: Examine Collins’s treatment of respectability and reputation.
essayQuestions.focus: Godfrey Ablewhite, Miss Clack, Rosanna Spearman and Ezra Jennings
plan: Pair the characters by reputation: the celebrated philanthropist and the reformatory housemaid, the tract-giver and the outcast assistant.
Show how suspicion is distributed in the First Period, and on what evidence.
Read Clack’s narrative for the mechanics of self-approval, using her own word ‘providentially’.
Use Cuff’s Sixth Narrative to establish what Godfrey’s public character was actually financed by.
Close on Jennings, who asks for consent and asks for nothing else, and on what the novel does with him.

discussionQuestions: Rachel knows the answer from the first morning and says nothing. Is her silence admirable, or does the novel punish her for it?
Betteredge consults Robinson Crusoe as an oracle. What does Collins gain by putting one famous English story inside another?
Miss Clack is ridiculous and every fact she reports is true. How should a reader use a witness like that?
Ezra Jennings solves the case and dies asking only to be forgotten. Why does Collins give the solution to the man nobody will employ?
The diamond goes back to India and the English characters never learn how. Is that an ending or a refusal to end?

related.why: Collins’s earlier experiment with the same method, where the witnesses are assembled as though for a trial.
The detective story after Cuff: inference raised to a system, and a investigator who is never wrong.
Betteredge’s oracle, opened at random for guidance throughout the First Period and quoted by page number in the first line.
Another All the Year Round serial with a concealed benefactor and a fortune whose origins will not bear examination.
A later novel assembled from journals, letters and statements, and equally interested in what a dossier can prove.
